original_value: Attention-based models have shown to be effective in learning representations for sentence classification. They are typically equipped with multi-hop attention mechanism. However, existing multi-hop models still suffer from the problem of paying much attention to the most frequently noticed words, which might not be important to classify the current sentence. And there is a lack of explicitly effective way that helps the attention to be shifted out of a wrong part in the sentence. In this paper, we alleviate this problem by proposing a differentiated attentive learning model. It is composed of two branches of attention subnets and an example discriminator. An explicit signal with the loss information of the first attention subnet is passed on to the second one to drive them to learn different attentive preference. The example discriminator then selects the suitable attention subnet for sentence classification. Experimental results on real and synthetic datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our model.

result.paraphrase: Attention-based models have proven effective for learning sentence-classification representations, and they are usually equipped with a multi-hop attention mechanism. Still, existing multi-hop approaches tend to focus too heavily on the words noticed most often, even when those words are not important for classifying the current sentence. Moreover, there is no explicitly effective method for shifting attention away from an incorrect region of the sentence. To address this issue, we propose a differentiated attentive learning model. The model consists of two attention-subnet branches and an example discriminator. An explicit signal carrying the loss information from the first attention subnet is sent to the second subnet so that the two learn different attention preferences. The example discriminator then chooses the appropriate attention subnet for sentence classification. Experiments on real and synthetic datasets show that the model is effective.
